'''John Clarke''' (born 10 February 1942) is a British experimental [[physicist]] and Professor Emeritus at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Clarke, Professor Emeritus of the Graduate School {{!}} Physics |url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/john-clarke |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008043838/https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/john-clarke |archive-date=8 October 2025 |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=physics.berkeley.edu}}</ref> He is known for his various works on measurement devices based on [[superconductivity]]. [[Steven Girvin]] has called Clarke "the godfather of superconducting electronics."<ref>{{Cite news |date=7 October 2025 |title=Nobel Prize in Physics Is Awarded for Work in Quantum Mechanics |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/07/science/nobel-prize-physics.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007113232/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/07/science/nobel-prize-physics.html |archive-date=7 October 2025 |access-date=9 October 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

In the 1980s, Clarke led a research team that included [[John M. Martinis]] and [[Michel Devoret]].<ref name=":1" /> Their discoveries in [[macroscopic quantum phenomena]] using the [[Josephson effect]] earned them the [[2025 Nobel Prizes|Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2025.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=7 October 2025 |title=AIP Congratulates 2025 Nobel Prize Winners in Physics - AIP.ORG |url=https://www.aip.org/aip/aip-congratulates-2025-nobel-prize-winners-in-physics |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007132009/https://www.aip.org/aip/aip-congratulates-2025-nobel-prize-winners-in-physics |archive-date=7 October 2025 |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=AIP |language=en}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
John Clarke was born on 10 February 1942 in [[Cambridge]], England.<ref name=Nobel>{{cite web |title=John Clarke – Facts |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/clarke/facts/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007130839/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/clarke/facts/ |archive-date=7 October 2025 |access-date=7 October 2025 |publisher=NobelPrize.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Clarke, John |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11504003.html |url-status=dead |publisher=American Institute of Physics |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241207011028/https://history.aip.org/phn/11504003.html |archive-date=7 December 2024 |access-date=7 October 2025}}</ref> He attended [[The Perse School]], before going to study [[Natural Sciences Tripos|Natural Sciences]] at [[Christ's College, Cambridge]], where he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1964.<ref name=timesnownews/><ref name=berkeley/>

In 1965, Clarke became one of the first students to enter the newly-founded [[Darwin College, Cambridge]], and was the first president of the Darwin College students' association.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darwin.cam.ac.uk/60th/anniversary/article/john-clarke-dcsa-president-1966-67/|title=John Clarke: DCSA President 1966–67|website=darwin.cam.ac.uk|date=July 2024 |access-date=7 October 2025}}</ref> While conducting his doctoral work under [[Brian Pippard]], Clarke developed a very sensitive [[voltmeter]], which he later called "SLUG" (Superconducting Low-inductance Undulatory Galvanometer).<ref name="timesnownews">{{cite web|url=https://www.timesnownews.com/education/cambridge-celebrates-its-126th-nobel-laureate-as-alumnus-john-clarke-wins-2025-physics-prize-article-152957573|title=Cambridge Celebrates Its 126th Nobel Laureate as Alumnus John Clarke Wins 2025 Physics Prize|website=Times Now|date=7 October 2025}}</ref><ref name=berkeley>{{Cite web |title=John Clarke, Professor Emeritus of the Graduate School |url=http://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/John-Clarke |url-status=live |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007131525/https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/John-Clarke |archive-date=7 October 2025 |access-date=7 October 2025}}</ref> He obtained a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1968.<ref name="berkeley" /> Clarke has said at various times that his work was influenced by Nobel laureate [[Brian Josephson]], who predicted the [[Josephson effect]] in 1962 and was also a previous student of Pippard.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rogalla |first1=Horst |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fnbRBQAAQBAJ&dq=pippard+clarke+brian+josephson&pg=PA321 |title=100 Years of Superconductivity |last2=Kes |first2=Peter H. |date=11 November 2011 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-4398-4948-4 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/clarke/interview/ |access-date=9 October 2025 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

After completing his doctorate, Clarke gained a postdoctoral research position at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and subsequently worked at Berkeley for his whole academic career, as Assistant Professor (1969), Associate Professor (1971), and as Professor of Physics (1973–2010).<ref name="Christs">{{cite web|url=https://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/college/people/fellows/professor-john-clarke|title=Professor John Clarke FRS|access-date=7 October 2025|website=christs.cam.ac.uk}}</ref>  In 1969, Clarke also joined  [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], eventually retiring as a faculty senior scientist in the Materials Sciences Division in 2010.<ref name="LBNL">{{cite web|url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2025/10/07/former-berkeley-lab-scientist-john-clarke-wins-2025-nobel-prize-in-physics/ |title=Former Berkeley Lab Scientist John Clarke Wins 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics |date=24 October 2025 |website=LBL.gov |language=en-US}}</ref>

Clarke's association with the [[University of Cambridge]] continued, after he moved to the United States. In 1972, he was elected a Fellow of Christ's College; in 1989, he was a visiting fellow at [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]], and in 1998 was elected a by-fellow of [[Churchill College, Cambridge]]. Clarke was awarded a [[Doctor of Science]] from the University of Cambridge in 2003. He was elected an Honorary Fellow of Christ's College in 1997, and of Darwin College in  2023.<ref name=Christs/>

== Research ==
Clarke's research focuses on [[superconductivity]] and superconducting electronics, particularly in the development and application of [[SQUID|superconducting quantum interference devices]] (SQUIDs), which are ultrasensitive detectors of [[magnetic flux]].<ref name="RS" /><ref name=Ford2005>{{cite book |last1=Ford |first1=P. J. |last2=Saunders |first2=G. A. |title=The Rise of the Superconductors |date=2005 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-203-64631-1 |page=169 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9JDgxu6BtrcC&pg=PA169 |language=en |chapter=9. Electron applications of high temperature super conductors}}</ref><ref name=Lakhani2025>{{cite book |last1=Lakhani |first1=Nikhil |title=Solid-State Physics: Core Principles |date=2025 |publisher=Educohack Press |isbn=978-93-6152-073-0 |page=138 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DZlIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PT138}}</ref>

In 1985, Clarke, [[John M. Martinis]] (his PhD student), and [[Michel Devoret]] (a postdoctoral researcher at the time) demonstrated the quantum behaviour of a [[Josephson effect|Josephson junction]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Hassinger |first=Sebastian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cE8hEQAAQBAJ&dq=martinis+phd+%22advisor%22+clarke+devoret&pg=PA113 |title=The New Quantum Era |date=11 September 2024 |publisher=O'Reilly Media, Inc. |isbn=978-1-0981-4938-3 |language=en}}</ref> They showed that at low temperature, a macroscopic electronic state associated with superconductors underwent [[quantum tunnelling]] at zero voltage.<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 October 2025 |title=What was the key experiment conducted by Michel H. Devoret, John Clarke, and John M. Martinis at Berkeley? {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/question/What-was-the-key-experiment-conducted-by-Michel-H-Devoret-John-Clarke-and-John-M-Martinis-at-Berkeley |access-date=9 October 2025 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref> The same year, by sending [[microwave]] pulses of the system, the [[phase qubit#Quantized energy levels|resonances showed quantised energy levels]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quantum effects in electrical circuits honored with Physics Nobel |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/physics-nobel-awarded-macro-demonstration-quantum-effects |access-date=9 October 2025 |website=www.science.org |language=en}}</ref> This experiment was the first evidence of [[circuit quantum electrodynamics]], that would become later the basis for [[superconducting quantum computing]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Blais |first1=Alexandre |last2=Grimsmo |first2=Arne L. |last3=Girvin |first3=S. M. |last4=Wallraff |first4=Andreas |date=19 May 2021 |title=Circuit quantum electrodynamics |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025005 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=93 |issue=2 |article-number=025005 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025005 |arxiv=2005.12667 |bibcode=2021RvMP...93b5005B }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=2020 |title=The ABC of cQED |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-020-0847-3 |journal=Nature Physics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=233 |doi=10.1038/s41567-020-0847-3 |bibcode=2020NatPh..16..233. |issn=1745-2481}}</ref> The work, which was recognized with the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2025, was largely funded by the Office of Basic Energy Sciences in the [[United States Department of Energy]].
<ref name="APS">{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2025/10/quiet-winner-nobel-prizes-science|title=The quiet winner of the Nobel Prizes in science|date=24 October 2025 |website=APS.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

Clarke has also worked in the application of SQUIDs configured as quantum-noise limited amplifiers to search for the [[axion]], a possible component of [[dark matter]].<ref name="RS">{{Cite web|title=Professor John Clarke FRS|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/john-clarke-11230/|url-status=live|publisher=Royal Society|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007130334/https://royalsociety.org/people/john-clarke-11230/|archive-date=2025-10-07|access-date=2017-06-15}}</ref>

== Recognition ==
Clarke obtained an [[Alfred P. Sloan]] fellowship (1970)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellows Database {{!}} Alfred P. Sloan Foundation |url=https://sloan.org/fellows-database |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=sloan.org |language=en}}</ref> and a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] (1977).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Guggenheim Fellowships: Supporting Artists, Scholars, & Scientists |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/john-clarke |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=www.gf.org}}</ref>
